To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the cellular organization and connectivity of the VMH are altered in SF-1KO mice and that the distribution of immunostaining for NPY, AgR, CART is altered.
the cellular organization and connections of the region of hypothalamus containing the VMH are disrupted in SF- 1 KO mice.
the cellular organization, the orientation of dendritic arbors, and neural connections to the VMH are altered in mice that lack the NR5a2 gene.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the cellular organization of hypothalamic nuclei that participate in energy balance.
the regulation of energy homeostasis and how the hypothalamus participates in this function.
understanding how the brain controls food intake and body weight.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the organization of the VMN is altered in the SF-1 KO mouse and that the changes in cell bodies, dendrites and fibers are consistent with changes in the regulation of body weight.
the organization of the ventromedinal region is altered in SF1 KO animals and that this change may contribute to the changes in feeding and body weight regulation that are seen in these mice.
the VMH is not a discrete cell group in mice lacking the NR5a gene and that the cellular organization is altered in SF-1 mice.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the cellular organization in the ventromedia hypothalamus is disrupted in mice with disruption of the NRSA1 gene.
the VMH is not a discrete cell group but rather a continuum of cells and projections that may be altered in SF-1KO mice.
SF-1 is required for normal development and function of hypothalamic neurons that regulate body weight and metabolism.
The main takeaway from our work is that
disruption of the NRs5a1 gene in mice leads to a reorganization of the ventromedinal nucleus of the hypothalamic region.
SF-1 KO animals have a rearrangement of the ventromedical hypothalamic area (VMH) which is a region that is critical to energy balance.
the organization and connectivity of the region of VMH in mice is disrupted as a result of the loss of SF-1 and this may account for the altered body weight regulation observed in these mice.
